slides.text: The Blackwood Tower had forty floors of glass and steel, but elevator three had a mechanical quirk that every graveyard-shift security guard knew by heart: at precisely 3:17 AM, it would ascend autonomously to the 23rd floor, hold its doors open for thirty seconds into total darkness, and descend. The 23rd floor was an empty concrete shell—raw wiring, no drywall, boarded windows, abandoned after a construction fatality in 1994. Guards joked it was just a glitch in the relay board.

On a rainy Tuesday, rookie night guard Sam decided to check the elevator’s internal weight sensor log. To his shock, every night at 3:17 AM when the doors opened on floor 23, the cabin's hydraulic pressure dropped by exactly one hundred and sixty pounds. Something—or someone—was stepping off. Sam pulled up the surveillance camera feed inside the elevator cabin for that exact minute. The video showed an empty car. But when the doors slid open, wet footprints appeared on the linoleum floor, leading out into the dark.

Tonight, Sam rode car three himself at 3:15 AM, clutching his heavy Maglite and service revolver. The lift groaned upward and jolted to a halt at floor 23. The stainless-steel doors parted. Sam shone his beam into the cavernous, dusty void. Across the raw concrete floor stood twenty-nine identical office chairs arranged in a neat semicircle, each occupied by a fresh, unread copy of tomorrow morning's newspaper. On the front page of every copy was Sam’s own obituary.
